body.en:
• Inheritance lets one class (child/subclass) acquire the members of another (parent/superclass) with extends: the child is born with the parent's fields and methods.
  • Write it as an IS-A sentence: Employee IS-A Person. If the sentence is true in real life, inheritance is the right tool.
  • Need: reusability (write common code once), extensibility (a child only adds its specialities) and maintainability (fix once in the parent - 200 children heal instantly).
  • Access rules: public/protected members flow freely; private members exist in the object but cannot be named directly by the child; constructors are never inherited.

Run jv3_1: Employee uses intro() although it never wrote it - that is the whole miracle in one line.

• Single: one parent, one child - Person -> Employee.
  • Multilevel: a chain of generations - Person -> Employee -> Manager; the grandchild receives everything from both.
  • Hierarchical: one parent, many children - Vehicle -> Car, Bike (the most common real-world shape).
  • Hybrid: a mixture of the above.
  • Multiple (two class parents) is NOT supported in Java: if both parents defined the same field or method, the child could not choose. The same effect is obtained with interfaces (3.3).

h.en: The super Keyword and Constructor Chaining

body.en:
• super inside a child refers to the parent part of the object.
  • super(args) calls the parent's constructor and must be the first statement of the child constructor; constructors always run top-down (parent first).
  • If the parent has ONLY parameterized constructors, the child must call super(...) explicitly - otherwise a compile error.
  • super.method() calls the parent's version of an overridden method; super.field reads a hidden parent field.
  • Rule of thumb: this = current object, super = its parent.

• Overriding: a child gives its own body to a method it inherited - same name, same parameters. Objective: specialisation (a LaserPrinter prints its own header).
  • Contrast with overloading (Unit 2): same name, different parameters, same class.
  • Rules: the signature must match; the return type must match (or be a subclass); the new method must not be MORE private than the inherited one; static methods cannot be overridden (they are hidden, not overridden); private and final methods cannot be overridden either.
  • Add @Override for free signature checking by the compiler.

• A parent reference may hold any child object: Shape sh = new Circle();.
  • For an overridden method, the JVM decides at run time which version to run by looking at the real object behind the reference - not the reference type.
  • This is the meaning of run-time (dynamic) polymorphism; overloading was the compile-time version.
  • Why it matters: you can loop over Shape[] and every shape still answers with its own area.

• final variable - a constant: assigned once, then read-only (naming convention: WHEELS, PI in capitals).
  • final method - a subclass inherits it but CANNOT override it - the behaviour stays identical for all children.
  • final class - cannot be extended at all; String and Math are famous final classes (protects them from being changed at runtime).

Practical 11 runs in jv3_7 - uncomment the error lines in the lab to see the compiler refuse.

• An abstract method declares WHAT without HOW: abstract double area(); - no braces, no body.
  • A class with at least one abstract method must itself be declared abstract; an abstract class cannot be instantiated (no new Shape()).
  • Rules of an abstract class: it may mix abstract and ready-made concrete methods, may hold any fields and constructors; a subclass extending it MUST implement every abstract method or declare itself abstract.
  • Use it for "half-built blueprints": share the common parts (displayType), force the special parts (area) on children.

Practical 10(a) builds exactly the syllabus's Shape with abstract area() and concrete displayType() - run jv3_8.

• An interface is a pure contract: method declarations with no state. Need: when different classes must promise the same ability without being related by a family tree (a Printer and a Phone can both be Callable).
  • Declaration: interface Drawable { void draw(); } - methods are implicitly public abstract; fields are implicitly public static final (constants).
  • Implementation: implements keyword; the class must give public bodies for every method, or declare itself abstract.
  • Interfaces cannot be instantiated, but references are allowed: Drawable d = new Circle(); - the object's own draw() runs (dynamic dispatch).
  • Abstract class vs interface table - the diagram.

h.en: Multiple Inheritance and Default/Static Methods in Interfaces

body.en:
• Class-level multiple inheritance is banned, but a class may implement any number of interfaces: class Report implements Printable, Showable - safe because interface methods carry no state and no default body clashes.
  • Java 8 added default methods with bodies inside interfaces: ready-made behaviour that every implementer inherits for free; and static methods invoked on the interface name.
  • If two interfaces offer the same default method, the class must override it - diamond conflicts are solved explicitly, never silently.

• A package is a named family of classes stored in a matching folder: it prevents name clashes, shapes access control (default and protected are package-scoped) and keeps projects navigable.
  • Defining: first line of the file: package college; - the file lives in a folder named college.
  • Importing: import college.Student; for one class, import java.util.*; for many, or the fully qualified name with no import at all: java.util.Date.
  • Built-in packages: java.lang (String, Math, Object - imported automatically), java.util (Scanner, ArrayList, Date), java.io (files), java.time (dates).

Practical 12 (jv3_12) creates the college package with a real Student class and imports it from Main - watch both files in the program window.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Ravi, age 35
pay = 42000.0
Ravi earns 42000.0

expl.en:
Practical 9 (part 1). With extends, the child class receives ALL fields and methods of the parent (except private ones and constructors).

  • Employee e = new Employee() has intro(), work(), name, age AND salary - as if the parent's code were copied in.
  • This relation is written Employee IS-A Person - inheritance models real "is a" facts.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
I am Ravi
I work for 42000.0
I lead Computer

expl.en:
Practical 9 (part 2). Multilevel inheritance: Parent -> Child -> Grandchild. A Manager gets the members of both Person and Employee in one step.

  • The chain is unlimited: every level passes everything it has (and got) further down.
  • Constructors also run in order Person -> Employee -> Manager when a Manager is created (see jv3_4 with super).

title.en: Types of inheritance: single, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
car: vehicle
bike: vehicle
petrol = vehicle

expl.en:
• Single: one parent, one child (Person -> Employee).
  • Multilevel: a chain of generations (Car -> PetrolCar).
  • Hierarchical: one parent, many children (Vehicle -> Car, Bike).
  • Hybrid: a mix of the above (allowed).
  • Multiple (two parents for one class) is NOT allowed for classes in Java - fields/methods would clash. The same effect is done with interfaces (see jv3_10).

title.en: The super keyword: constructor chaining and parent methods

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Shape: circle
I am a 2D shape
radius = 2.5

expl.en:
• super(...) calls the parent constructor and must be the first statement of the child constructor. If the parent has only parameterized constructors, the child MUST call super(...) itself.
  • super.method() explicitly calls the parent's version of a method - essential when the child overrides it.
  • super.field reads the parent's field when names clash.
  • Watch the output order: the parent's constructor runs before the child's body - top-down construction.

• Overloading = same name, different parameter list, same class (compile-time choice).
  • Overriding = same name AND same signature in a child class; the child's version replaces the parent's at run time.
  • @Override is an optional annotation - the compiler then refuses to compile if you mistyped the signature.
  • The child method cannot be more private than the parent's (e.g. public -> private is an error).

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
area = 78.5
area = 16.0

expl.en:
• A parent reference may point to a child object: Shape sh = new Circle();.
  • When an overridden method is called through that reference, Java looks at the actual object (Circle / Square) - not at the reference type - and runs the child's version.
  • This is dynamic method dispatch = run-time polymorphism; the choice happens while the program executes.
  • It is the engine behind flexible designs: one variable, many behaviours.

title.en: The final keyword: variable, method, class

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
wheels = 2
service done
peep

expl.en:
Practical 11. final = "end of change", with three seats:

  • final variable - a constant: assigned once, then read-only.
  • final method - subclasses inherit it but cannot override it.
  • final class - cannot be extended at all (String itself is final!).
  • The commented-out lines would produce real compile errors - try them in lab.

title.en: Abstract class Shape with abstract method area()

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Type: rectangle
area = 60.0

expl.en:
Practical 10 (part 1).

  • An abstract method has only a declaration - no body; any subclass must implement it or be abstract itself.
  • An abstract class mixes abstract and normal methods (displayType is ready-made); it cannot be instantiated - no new Shape().
  • Use it to force a common contract ("every shape has an area") while sharing concrete code.

title.en: Interface Drawable implemented by Circle and Rectangle

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
O  (circle)
[ ] (rectangle)
UNIT = 20

expl.en:
Practical 10 (part 2).

  • An interface declares what to do, never how: methods are implicitly public abstract, fields are implicitly public static final (constants).
  • A class implements an interface and must write a public body for every method; it may also extend another class at the same time (as Circle and Rectangle do).
  • Interface references work like parent references: Drawable d1 = new Circle(); dispatches to the object's draw().

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
printing...
showing...

expl.en:
• Classes get only ONE parent, but interfaces are unlimited: implements Printable, Showable.
  • No clash can happen, because interface methods carry no state and (normally) no body - the child provides the single implementation either way.
  • This is how Java supplies multiple inheritance safely.

title.en: Default and static methods in an interface (Java 8+)

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
== shape maths ==
I have area 16.0

expl.en:
• Since Java 8 interfaces may hold default methods with bodies - inherited by every implementing class without rewriting.
  • static methods in interfaces belong to the interface itself and are called as ShapeMath.banner().
  • If two interfaces offer the same default method, the class must override it to resolve the conflict (the diamond rule).

title.en: User-defined package: create, import and use

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
roll = 12
name = Pooja
I am Pooja

expl.en:
Practical 12. A package is a named folder for related classes - it avoids name clashes and makes imports possible.

  • The class file writes package college; first and sits inside a folder named college.
  • Main.java takes it in with import college.Student;. Without import, its full name college.Student would be needed.
  • Members used from another package must be public.
  • The compile line is javac college/Student.java Main.java and then java Main.

• Java ships hundreds of reusable packages: java.lang (String, Math, Object - auto-imported), java.util (Scanner, ArrayList, Date), java.io, java.net, java.time ...
  • java.lang is special: it is always available without an import statement.
  • For every other package write import java.util.Date; or use the wildcard import java.util.*;.
  • Package names are lower case by convention.

title.en: Cross-package access: protected fields in subclasses

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
roll = 1
name = Meera

expl.en:
• protected members are visible inside the package AND inside any subclass, even in a different package.
  • Here Student (package college) has protected fields; class Topper in the default package extends it and reads roll and name directly.
  • Without extends, protected fields would be invisible from the default package - that is exactly the difference between default and protected.

terms.en: super = parent part; super() goes first
same signature; object decides at run time

items.f:
final int WHEELS = 2;     // constant
final void service() { }  // no override
final class Pet { }       // no subclass

terms.en: final = constant / frozen method / sealed class
child must implement or be abstract
default = inheritable body; static = on interface
many interfaces OK, one class parent only
first line package; import before class
java.lang is automatic; others need import

q.en: What is inheritance?

a.en: A mechanism in which a new class (child/subclass) acquires the fields and methods of an existing class (parent/superclass) using extends.

q.en: Give the need of inheritance.

a.en: Reusability of tested code, easy extension by adding only specialities, and single-point maintenance in the parent.

q.en: What is an IS-A relationship?

a.en: Employee IS-A Person: if the sentence is true in real life, let Employee extend Person.

q.en: Which keyword creates inheritance?

a.en: extends for classes; implements for interfaces.

q.en: What does a child NOT inherit?

a.en: Private members (they exist but cannot be named) and constructors.

q.en: List the types of inheritance in Java.

a.en: Single, multilevel, hierarchical, hybrid; multiple (two class parents) is NOT supported.

q.en: Why is multiple inheritance of classes banned?

a.en: If both parents had the same field or method the child would face ambiguity; interfaces solve it without state.

q.en: What is multilevel inheritance?

a.en: A chain A -> B -> C; C receives members of both A and B (Person -> Employee -> Manager).

q.en: What is hierarchical inheritance?

a.en: One parent, many children - Vehicle -> Car, Bike.

q.en: What is the super keyword?

a.en: Reference to the parent part of the object: super(args) calls the parent constructor, super.method() the parent method, super.field a hidden field.

q.en: Where must super() be written and why?

a.en: As the first statement of the child constructor; the parent part must be built before the child's body runs.

q.en: What happens if the parent has only parameterized constructors?

a.en: Java cannot silently add super() - the child must call super(args) explicitly, else compile error.

q.en: What is method overriding?

a.en: A child redefines an inherited method with the SAME name and signature so its own version runs instead.

q.en: Overriding vs overloading?

a.en: Same signature in child class, run-time, vs different parameters in one class, compile-time.

q.en: What is @Override?

a.en: An annotation asking the compiler to verify the method actually overrides one - catches signature typos.

q.en: Which methods cannot be overridden?

a.en: static (they are hidden, not overridden), private (not visible) and final methods.

q.en: What is dynamic method dispatch?

a.en: Calling an overridden method through a parent reference - the JVM runs the version of the actual object at run time.

q.en: Give an example of run-time polymorphism.

a.en: Shape sh = new Circle(); sh.area(); - Circle's area runs although the reference is typed Shape.

q.en: What are the three uses of final?

a.en: final variable = constant; final method = cannot be overridden; final class = cannot be extended.

q.en: Why is String a final class?

a.en: So no subclass can change string behaviour after an object is created - protects shared literals.

q.en: What is an abstract method?

a.en: A declaration without a body: abstract double area(); - the child provides the body.

q.en: What is an abstract class? Can it be instantiated?

a.en: A class declared abstract, possibly with abstract methods; no - new Shape() is a compile error.

q.en: Give the rules of abstract classes.

a.en: May mix abstract and concrete methods; may have fields/constructors; a subclass must implement every abstract method or be abstract too.

q.en: When do you choose an abstract class?

a.en: For a family blueprint that shares ready-made code (displayType) yet forces children to fill in specifics (area).

q.en: What is an interface?

a.en: A pure contract of method declarations (implicitly public abstract) plus constants (public static final); no state, no constructors.

q.en: What is the need of an interface?

a.en: Unrelated classes promising the same ability - a Printer and a Phone can both be Callable without sharing a parent.

q.en: How does a class implement an interface?

a.en: class X implements Drawable { public void draw() { } } - every method must be given a public body.

q.en: Why must an implemented method be public?

a.en: Interface methods are public abstract; an implementing method cannot reduce visibility.

q.en: Can an interface be instantiated? What about a reference?

a.en: Never instantiated; but Drawable d = new Circle(); works - the object's draw() runs.

q.en: What is multiple inheritance with interfaces?

a.en: Implementing several interfaces at once - safe because interfaces have no state or clashing bodies.

q.en: What are default methods in interfaces?

a.en: Java 8+ interface methods with bodies, inherited free by every implementer; the class may override them.

q.en: What happens if two interfaces give the same default method?

a.en: The implementing class must override it and resolve the conflict - Java never picks silently.

q.en: What are static methods in interfaces?

a.en: Methods belonging to the interface itself, called as ShapeMath.banner(); not inherited into instances.

q.en: Abstract class vs interface: three differences.

a.en: Fields any vs constants only; constructor yes vs no; one parent class vs many interfaces.

q.en: What is a package?

a.en: A named group of related classes in a matching folder; controls name clashes and access (default/protected are package-based).

q.en: How do you define and import your own package?

a.en: Write package college; in college/Student.java, then import college.Student; in the user file.

q.en: Name three built-in packages.

a.en: java.lang (String, Math - automatic), java.util (Scanner, ArrayList), java.io (files); also java.time.

q.en: Which package never needs an import?

a.en: java.lang.

q.en: What does import java.util.* mean?

a.en: Import every public class of java.util (the wildcard) - still per-name, not the whole library copied.

q.en: How must cross-package members be declared?

a.en: public (or protected for subclasses).

q.en: Is the fully-qualified name legal without import?

a.en: Yes: java.util.Date d = new java.util.Date(); - import is just a shortcut.

q.en: What is a hybrid inheritance example?

a.en: Vehicle -> Car -> PetrolCar plus Vehicle -> Bike: multilevel and hierarchical combined.

q.en: If a parent method is final, what about a useful child version?

a.en: Impossible by design - the child inherits the exact behaviour; redesign with a non-final method.

q.en: In Practical 10, why doesn't Drawable conflict with Shape?

a.en: Shape is the single parent class (state, constructors); Drawable only adds a promise (draw) with no state - no diamond problem.
